chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the blood money for intentional killing, so he said: One hundred from the mature camels (masan), and if there are no camels, then in place of each camel, twenty from the mature sheep.

As for what this narration includes regarding the difference in the ages of camels in cases of accidental and semi-intentional killing, and what the earlier narrations include, the way to understand it is that we interpret it as meaning the Imam has the discretion to act with whichever he chooses, according to what he sees in the situation as being more beneficial.

And as for what it includes that if there are no camels, then in place of each camel there are twenty sheep, this bears two meanings: One is that the blood money of camels is only incumbent upon the people of the desert (Bawadi), so whoever from them refuses to give the camels, it is permissible to take from them in place of each camel twenty sheep at their valuation.
And the other meaning is that we interpret it as applying to a slave who killed a free person, for that is incumbent upon him if his guardians wish to pay the blood money on his behalf.
ai.seo_question: What is the prescribed blood money for intentional homicide in Shia jurisprudence and how is it calculated if camels are unavailable?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the fixed *diyah* for intentional homicide as one hundred mature camels, resolving apparent contradictions in other texts by attributing variations to the Imam's discretionary authority (*ra'y*) based on public interest (*maslaha*). The text further elucidates the substitution mechanism—replacing one camel with twenty sheep—by offering two scholarly interpretations: either it applies to desert dwellers who refuse to provide camels, or it pertains to the compensation for a slave killing a free person, highlighting the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence in applying fixed rulings to diverse social contexts.
